title_original: Thames & Hudson : Joséphine Seblon : Mini Photographers

blocks.text: The image of a child in a famous photograph by Diane Arbus hardly provides an affirmative picture of childhood and conventional readings of an equally famous novel, William Golding’s Lord of the Flies , point to a correspondingly bleak view of children’s potential. The novel, about a group of children left to fend for themselves on a deserted island, is conventionally read as depicting a reversion to a savage and violent herd mentality that lurks within human nature.

But there is another way to interpret Lord of the Flies , one tracing the conformism and violence that develop on the island to differences in the class backgrounds and upbringings of those stranded there. There are also photographers like Helen Levitt whose portrayals of childhood are very different to those of Golding and Arbus. Levitt captures a natural capacity for ludic expressiveness on the part of juveniles and she does this without falling into the trap of sentimentality that pictures children as angelic, gendered innocents.

Mini Photographers happily waves a flag on the side of Levitt by addressing children and encouraging them to channel their creative playfulness through photography. Illustrated by Vivian Maier’s Self-Portrait (1953) – where she stands with her camera next to a child as they both look, emboldened, at their reflection in a shop window – the author’s introduction points out that a self-portrait can be more than a selfie. A photograph, she acclaims, can be a crafted piece of art and famous photographs can be used as springboards for experiments: ‘I can guarantee that as you train your eye, you’ll never see the world in the same way again’.

Following ‘tech tips’, suggesting to its young audience that they consider going beyond reliance on a smartphone for their picture-taking, Mini Photographers divides into different sections based around past, modern and contemporary photographers. Each section uses a notable photograph to launch practical ideas for playing with a particular idea or technique with their camera and the author’s own inventiveness is admirable. Photographers from the past include Man Ray’s ‘cheeky’ (is the author enjoying her own ‘childish’ wordplay?) Le Violon d’Ingres – deployed in a ‘get surreal’ mini project by suggesting the reader takes acrylic paint pens to add butterfly wings to a photo of a friend or a moustache to one of a sibling, André Kertész’s Shadow, Paris , shown to provoke interest in photographing shadows (a ‘cake rack, a fish slice or a colander perhaps?’), Ilse Bing’s Self-Portrait in Mirrors for using a mirror for a double self-portrait and Saul Leiter’s Red Umbrella for the possibilities of photographing in bad weather and snapping reflections in puddles.

The section on ‘modern’ photographers is just as lively and resourceful with Philippe Halsman’s Marilyn Monroe for motion shots and Jean-Paul Goude’s Cubist Grace for fashion shoots. The ‘contemporary’ photography section stretches children’s imagination with proposals for ways to question convention: Hendrik and Paula Kerstens’ Paper Roll seems bound to appeal to children’s mischievous sense of humour.
An unintimidating, colourfully illustrated and hands-on guide like Mini Photographers is to be applauded for informally introducing the pleasure of photography to young people.
